metal_context: Late Bronze Age international arms system using bronze weapons, composite bows, chariots, and scale armor; iron was not the organizing material.
scale_scope: One expeditionary army approaching Kadesh; four divisions are recorded and the total is a modern inference from a proposed division size.
recruitment_system: Four named divisions coordinated by a territorial state and royal command system.
equipment_system: A mixed system of infantry, archery, chariots, armor, and imported or shared weapon traditions—not one metal advantage.
supply_system: Campaign routes, frontier forts, storage, ships, baggage, fodder, and water formed a logistical system beyond the weapon itself.
replacement_system: The selected evidence does not quantify annual replacement or a standing total.
interpretation: A large organized field force existed before an iron economy. The case makes institutions and supply visible as independent requirements.
limits: The Egyptian starting total is not directly stated. Approximately 20,000 is Breasted's inference from four divisions and the division size in Papyrus Anastasi I; it is not comparable to Taylor's whole-war strategic deployment models for Rome and Carthage.

metal_context: Iron lowered the cost of simple swords and spearheads, while helmets and body armor remained uneven and often concentrated among elites.
scale_scope: A broad and regionally uneven transition from aristocratic retinues toward larger client levies; not one army or dated census.
recruitment_system: Aristocrats and core retainers increasingly mobilized peasant clients through personal and civic social ties.
equipment_system: Cheaper iron could put simple weapons in more hands; it did not equalize armor, training, or status.
supply_system: Households, clients, communities, and local elites supplied men and materiel without a uniform bureaucratic train.
replacement_system: No definition-compatible series measures how long these forces could be sustained or replaced.
interpretation: Cheaper equipment plausibly widened the military participation margin, but external pressure and social organization also drove the transition.
limits: This is a specialist synthesis across diverse societies and centuries. Archaeological weapons do not reveal an army total, mobilization rate, or causal share for iron; the row therefore contains no numeric force estimate.

metal_context: Iron-age Mediterranean equipment assembled through Punic, subject, allied, and mercenary systems rather than one citizen equipment regime.
scale_scope: Modeled total strategic deployment across simultaneous theaters in 215 BCE.
recruitment_system: Most troops came from subject peoples, subaltern allies, or mercenaries; citizen contingents were a small part of the total.
equipment_system: Equipment came through several political and military relationships; the selected model does not estimate kilograms of metal per soldier.
supply_system: Imperial revenues, ports, allied obligations, and paid service supported forces dispersed across several theaters.
replacement_system: The peak is one modeled cross-section. It does not by itself measure the durability of Carthaginian replacement after losses.
interpretation: Carthage reached a peak close to Rome through a different recruitment architecture, showing that iron equipment alone does not identify the mobilization system.
limits: Approximately 170,000 is Taylor's reconstruction of strategic deployment, not one battlefield count or a surviving census. It is comparable here only with Taylor's Roman model and must not be combined with the Kadesh inference or the qualitative civitas case.

metal_context: Iron-age Mediterranean equipment distributed through citizen property classes, Latin colonies, and allied communities; armor remained unequal.
scale_scope: Modeled total strategic deployment across simultaneous theaters in 212 BCE; roughly twenty-five legions and allied formations.
recruitment_system: Roman citizens, Latin colonists, and socii served through a franchised system of levies and allied obligations.
equipment_system: Self-equipment and low pay shifted part of the material burden onto households and communities; the model contains no kilograms-per-soldier estimate.
supply_system: Italian farms, allied communities, state command, roads, fleets, pay, and requisitioning sustained armies across several theaters.
replacement_system: Rome maintained very high deployments after catastrophic losses, but this selected maximum is not an annual replacement curve.
interpretation: Rome's peak was institutional extraction from an unusually broad political-military network, not a direct output of abundant iron.
limits: Approximately 185,000 is Taylor's reconstruction of strategic deployment, not one battlefield count. Alternative scholarly totals exist, external auxiliaries are not fully included, and the 15,000 difference from Carthage is not visualized as a precision claim or victory margin.
